question: Explain the offences relating to summons under Sections 206, 207 and 208 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: These three sections protect the service and obedience of summonses, notices and orders issued by public servants legally competent to issue them. Section 206 (formerly s.172 IPC) punishes absconding in order to avoid being served. Section 207 (formerly s.173 IPC) punishes intentionally preventing service on oneself or another, preventing the lawful affixing of a summons, notice or order, removing it after it has been lawfully affixed, or preventing the lawful making of a proclamation. Section 208 (formerly s.174 IPC) punishes a person legally bound to attend a certain place and time, in person or by agent, who intentionally omits to attend or departs before he may lawfully leave; its Illustrations mention failing to obey a High Court subpoena and a witness failing to appear before a District Judge. All three follow the same two-tier scale: simple imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both; and where the summons, notice, order or proclamation requires attendance in a Court (or, under ss.206-207, production of a document or electronic record in a Court), simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both. All are non-cognizable, bailable, not compoundable and triable by any Magistrate. The common element is that the process must come from a public servant legally competent to issue it; defying an unauthorised summons is not an offence.

question: What is the offence under Section 209 of the BNS? How does it differ from Section 208?
modelAnswer: Section 209 (formerly s.174A IPC) punishes whoever fails to appear at the specified place and time as required by a proclamation published under BNSS s.84(1). BNSS s.84(1) allows a Court that has reason to believe a person against whom it has issued a warrant has absconded or is concealing himself, so that the warrant cannot be executed, to publish a written proclamation requiring him to appear at a specified place and time not less than thirty days from its publication. Failing to appear is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both, or community service. If the Court has also made a declaration under BNSS s.84(4) pronouncing him a proclaimed offender, the punishment is imprisonment up to seven years and fine. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. It differs from s.208 in several ways: s.208 covers ordinary non-attendance in obedience to any summons, notice, order or proclamation from a competent public servant, whereas s.209 deals with a person who is already evading a warrant and has been proclaimed; s.208 carries at most six months, s.209 up to three or seven years; and s.208 is non-cognizable and bailable, while s.209 is cognizable and non-bailable. The BNS adds community service as an alternative punishment for the basic s.209 offence.

question: Distinguish between Section 212 and Section 217 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Both punish giving false information to a public servant, but they differ. (1) Who can commit it: s.212 applies only to a person legally bound to furnish information on the subject to the public servant; s.217 applies to anyone who gives information, whether or not he was bound to. (2) Mental element: under s.212 it is enough that the person furnishes as true information he knows or has reason to believe is false; s.217 additionally requires that he intends, or knows it likely, that the public servant will do or omit something he would not if he knew the truth, or will use his lawful power to injure or annoy a person. (3) Purpose: s.212 protects the flow of information the law requires (for example from village officials about crimes); s.217 targets the misuse of public servants' power through false complaints. (4) Punishment: s.212 — simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both, and up to two years (either description) or fine where the information concerns an offence, its prevention or the apprehension of an offender; s.217 — up to one year, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Both are non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Illustrations: under s.212, a landholder who falsely reports a murder in his estate as a snakebite; under s.217, a person who falsely tells the police that someone has contraband, knowing a search will annoy him.

question: Explain Section 223 of the BNS (disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant). Why is the Explanation important?
modelAnswer: Section 223 (formerly s.188 IPC) punishes whoever, knowing that an order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate it directs him to abstain from a certain act, or to take certain order with property in his possession or management, disobeys that direction. Punishment depends on the consequence: (a) if the disobedience causes or tends to cause obstruction, annoyance or injury, or risk of it, to any person lawfully employed — simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹2,500, or both; (b) if it causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety, or causes or tends to cause a riot or affray — imprisonment of either description up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. It is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The ingredients are: a lawfully promulgated order by an empowered public servant; the accused's knowledge of it; disobedience; and the harm, or tendency to harm, specified in (a) or (b). The Explanation provides that the offender need not intend to cause harm or even contemplate harm; it is enough that he knows of the order and that his disobedience produces or is likely to produce harm. This makes the section effective for enforcing public-order measures, such as prohibitory orders under BNSS s.163, curfews or health restrictions, where the offender often honestly believes his conduct is harmless. The Gazette's Illustration: a person who knowingly takes a religious procession down a street in breach of a lawful order, and thereby causes danger of riot, commits the offence.

question: Discuss Section 226 of the BNS. How does the BNS treat attempted suicide compared with the IPC?
modelAnswer: Under the IPC, s.309 made any attempt to commit suicide punishable with simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both. That provision had long been criticised as punishing people in distress, and the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (s.115) already presumed that a person attempting suicide was under severe stress and should not be punished. The BNS does not re-enact s.309 at all, so a general attempt to commit suicide is no longer an offence. Instead, s.226 creates a narrow new offence: whoever attempts to commit suicide with the intent to compel or restrain any public servant from discharging his official duty is punishable with simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, or community service. It is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The ingredients are: an attempt to commit suicide; and the specific intent to compel a public servant, or restrain him from discharging his official duty. The section targets coercive tactics, such as attempted self-immolation to stop a demolition, eviction or arrest. Without that intent, attempting suicide is not punishable. Abetting suicide remains an offence under ss.107-108.

question: Explain the offences in Sections 213, 214 and 215 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: These three sections punish refusal to cooperate in truth-finding before a competent public servant. Section 213 (formerly s.178 IPC) punishes whoever refuses to bind himself by an oath or affirmation to state the truth when required to do so by a public servant legally competent to require it; a person may choose to affirm instead of taking a religious oath, but may not refuse both. Section 214 (formerly s.179 IPC) punishes whoever, being legally bound to state the truth on a subject to a public servant, refuses to answer a question on that subject demanded by the public servant in the exercise of his legal powers. This is subject to the protection against self-incrimination in Article 20(3) of the Constitution, which means an accused cannot be forced to answer questions that would incriminate him. Section 215 (formerly s.180 IPC) punishes whoever refuses to sign a statement he made when required to sign it by a public servant legally competent to require it; since BNSS s.181 forbids statements to the police during investigation from being signed, s.215 does not apply to them. Punishments: ss.213 and 214 — simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both; s.215 — simple imprisonment up to three months, or fine up to ₹3,000, or both. All are non-cognizable and bailable; they are triable by the Court in which the offence is committed, subject to Chapter XXVIII of the BNSS, or, if not committed in a Court, by any Magistrate.

question: What does Section 221 of the BNS punish? How does it relate to Section 132?
modelAnswer: Section 221 (formerly s.186 IPC) punishes whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, with imprisonment of either description up to three months, or fine up to ₹2,500, or both. It is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Its ingredients are: the victim is a public servant; he is discharging his public functions; and the accused voluntarily obstructs him. 'Obstruct' generally requires some act — physical or otherwise — that actually hinders the public servant, such as blocking his way, locking him out or snatching official papers; mere verbal protest or refusal to cooperate, without hindrance, is usually not enough. The function being performed must be a lawful public function. Section 132 (assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharge of his duty) is the aggravated counterpart: where the obstruction involves assault or criminal force, s.132 applies, with up to two years, and it is cognizable and non-bailable. So s.221 covers obstruction without violence, while s.132 covers obstruction by assault or criminal force.

question: Explain Sections 218, 219 and 220 of the BNS relating to property taken or sold by public authority.
modelAnswer: These sections protect the process by which public servants take and sell property, for example in executing court decrees or recovering public dues. Section 218 (formerly s.183 IPC) punishes whoever offers any resistance to the taking of any property by the lawful authority of a public servant, knowing or having reason to believe he is such a public servant: up to six months, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Section 219 (formerly s.184 IPC) punishes whoever intentionally obstructs any sale of property offered for sale by the lawful authority of a public servant: up to one month, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 220 (formerly s.185 IPC) punishes, at any such sale, purchasing or bidding on account of a person (oneself or another) whom one knows to be under a legal incapacity to purchase that property at that sale, or bidding without intending to perform the obligations the bid creates: up to one month, or fine up to ₹200, or both. All three are non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The taking or sale must be by lawful authority; resistance to an illegal seizure is not punishable under s.218. Section 220 complements s.203, which punishes a public servant who is himself barred from buying certain property.

question: Problem: M files a written complaint with the police alleging that his business rival N has kidnapped M's nephew, knowing this is false, in the hope that N will be arrested. The police raid N's house. Later, called before the Magistrate, M refuses to take an oath. Discuss M's liability under Chapter XIII.
modelAnswer: False complaint: M gave the police information he knew to be false, intending that they would use their lawful power (a raid and arrest) to the injury or annoyance of N. This satisfies s.217(b): imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Section 212 does not apply because M was not legally bound to furnish the information; he volunteered it. Depending on the facts, M may also be liable under Chapter XIV for falsely charging a person with an offence with intent to injure him, which is more serious; s.217 would then be an alternative or additional charge. Refusing the oath: when the Magistrate, a public servant legally competent to require an oath or affirmation, requires M to bind himself to state the truth and M refuses, he commits the offence under s.213: simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. If M had instead taken the oath and repeated the false allegation, he would have been liable under s.216 (false statement on oath, up to three years and fine) or for giving false evidence in a judicial proceeding under s.229. Both s.217 and s.213 are non-cognizable and bailable.

question: Problem: The District Magistrate issues a lawful order under BNSS s.163 prohibiting any gathering of more than five persons near a disputed site. P, knowing of the order, holds a meeting of forty people there, believing it would be peaceful. Stones are thrown and a fight breaks out. Police disperse the crowd. Discuss P's liability under Section 223.
modelAnswer: Section 223 requires: (1) an order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate it — here the District Magistrate's order under BNSS s.163, which allows a Magistrate to direct any person to abstain from a certain act; (2) that the accused knew of the order — P knew; (3) disobedience — P held a gathering of forty people in breach of it; and (4) that the disobedience caused or tended to cause the harm specified. The gathering led to stone-throwing and a fight, so it caused or tended to cause danger to human safety and a riot or affray, bringing it within clause (b): imprisonment of either description up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. P's belief that the meeting would be peaceful is no defence: under the Explanation, it is not necessary that the offender intend or contemplate harm; it is enough that he knows of the order and his disobedience produces, or is likely to produce, harm. The offence is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Depending on the facts, P and others may also be liable under Chapter XI — for example, if the gathering became an unlawful assembly and rioting occurred (ss.189-191).
